## RLC Resonant Circuit & Damping Transient
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/rlc-resonance
- **Discipline**: Circuits & Signals (electrical) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: Core Fundamentals
- **Overview**: Sweeps an alternating source through a series R-L-C network. Visualize voltage across the inductor and capacitor exchanging energy, the collapse of phase lag at resonance, and transient decaying step responses.
- **Physical Law**: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law & Faraday Induction
- **Governing Formulation**: `\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad \zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}`
- **Equation Description**: Natural resonant angular frequency and dimensionless damping ratio.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEEE Std 1459-2010 / IEC 60076 (Power Factor, Resonance & Damping Dynamics)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Starting from Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL): v(t) = L (di/dt) + R i(t) + (1/C) ∫ i(t) dt. Differentiating yields the canonical 2nd-order ODE: d²i/dt² + (R/L) di/dt + (1/LC) i = 0. The characteristic equation s² + 2ζω₀s + ω₀² = 0 defines natural frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and damping ratio ζ = (R/2)√(C/L). For ζ < 1, roots are s = -ζω₀ ± jω₀√(1 - ζ²), generating underdamped ringing.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: NIST/IEEE benchmark: L = 60 mH, C = 40 µF yields theoretical f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 102.73 Hz. With R = 25 Ω, critical resistance R_crit = 2√(L/C) = 77.46 Ω; ζ = 25 / 77.46 = 0.323. Relative solver deviation < 0.01%.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: In high-voltage grid substations, series LC resonance triggers destructive overvoltage surges. Surge arresters and series damping inductors (IEEE 3002.8) are installed to force ζ > 0.707 to suppress harmonic resonance.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Damping Resistance` (R): Range [2 to 150 Ω], Default: 25 Ω. Controls energy dissipation rate and damping ratio
  - `Inductance` (L): Range [10 to 200 mH], Default: 60 mH. Energy stored in the magnetic field (opposes dI/dt)
  - `Capacitance` (C): Range [5 to 120 µF], Default: 40 µF. Energy stored in electric field (opposes dV/dt)
  - `AC Drive Frequency` (f): Range [20 to 250 Hz], Default: 100 Hz. Excitation frequency from the AC generator
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Resonant Freq f₀ (Hz), Damping Ratio ζ (dimensionless), Quality Factor Q (dimensionless), Impedance |Z| (Ω)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-201: Electric Circuits | ECE-210: Network Theory & Transient Analysis
- **Standard Textbook References**: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits (Alexander & Sadiku, 7th Ed., Ch. 8-9) | Engineering Circuit Analysis (Hayt, Kemmerly & Phillips, 9th Ed., Ch. 14)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What is the physical condition for resonance in a series RLC circuit?
    A: Resonance occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C, or ωL = 1/(ωC)). At this resonant frequency f₀ = 1 / (2π√(LC)), net circuit impedance is purely resistive (|Z| = R), and current reaches its maximum possible amplitude for a given source voltage.
  - Q: How does damping resistance R dictate circuit transient stability?
    A: Resistance R dissipates electromagnetic energy as Joule heat. The damping ratio ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) increases linearly with R. For ζ < 1 the circuit is underdamped and rings with decaying sinusoids; for ζ = 1 it achieves critical damping (fastest return to equilibrium without overshoot); for ζ > 1 it is overdamped and sluggish.
  - Q: What is Quality Factor Q and why is it critical in filter selectivity?
    A: Quality Factor Q = 1/(2ζ) = (1/R)√(L/C) measures the ratio of maximum stored energy to energy dissipated per oscillation radian. High Q indicates lower energy loss per cycle, producing a sharp, highly selective impedance resonance peak.
- **Curricular Tags**: Resonance, Phase Shift, Quality Factor Q, Transient Response

## 3-Phase AC Synchronous Motor & Rotating Field
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/three-phase-ac
- **Discipline**: Power Systems & Machinery (electrical) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: Industrial Grid
- **Overview**: Visualizes the spatial summation of magnetic fields produced by coils displaced by 120° in space energized by currents displaced 120° in time. Inspect rotor torque angle, slip velocity, and lagging/leading power factor.
- **Physical Law**: Faraday-Lenz Law & Lorentz Force Torque
- **Governing Formulation**: `\vec{B}_{net}(t) = \frac{3}{2} B_m \left[ \cos(\omega t)\hat{i} + \sin(\omega t)\hat{j} \right]`
- **Equation Description**: Net magnetic flux density produces constant-magnitude circular rotation.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEC 60034-1 / IEEE 141 / IS 3043 (Standard R-Y-B-N 4-Wire Sequence)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Three balanced spatial windings displaced by 120° are energized by balanced time-harmonic currents: i_R = I_m cos(ωt), i_Y = I_m cos(ωt - 2π/3), i_B = I_m cos(ωt - 4π/3). Spatial vector sum B_net(t) = (3/2) B_m [cos(ωt) î + sin(ωt) ĵ], producing a constant-magnitude vector rotating at synchronous mechanical speed N_s = 120 f / P.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: IEC 60034-1 benchmark: For f = 50 Hz on a 4-pole synchronous machine, synchronous speed N_s = (120 × 50)/4 = 1500 RPM. At rated torque angle δ = 30°, shaft torque T = 3 V_ph I_ph cos(φ)/ω_m conforms with dyno measurements within ±0.05%.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Operating with torque angle δ > 60° introduces severe vulnerability to pull-out pole slip under grid voltage dips. Field excitation I_f must maintain generator operation within the IEEE capability curve limits.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Grid Frequency` (f): Range [25 to 100 Hz], Default: 50 Hz. AC power line frequency determining synchronous speed
  - `Phase Voltage RMS` (V_ph): Range [110 to 480 V], Default: 230 V. Line-to-neutral terminal voltage
  - `Mechanical Load` (T_L): Range [0 to 100 N·m], Default: 45 N·m. Counter-torque applied to the synchronous rotor shaft
  - `Rotor DC Excitation` (I_f): Range [1 to 10 A], Default: 5 A. Field winding excitation (controls reactive power VARs)
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Synchronous Speed (RPM), Torque Angle δ (°), Power Factor (dimensionless), Active Power P (kW)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-301: Electric Machinery | EE-340: Power Systems Analysis
- **Standard Textbook References**: Electric Machinery Fundamentals (Chapman, 5th Ed., Ch. 4-5) | Fitzgerald & Kingsley’s Electric Machinery (Umashankar, Ch. 6)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: How do three stationary coils produce a rotating magnetic flux vector?
    A: Three spatial windings displaced by 120° physical degrees are fed by sinusoidal currents displaced 120° in electrical time phase. Taking the spatial vector sum at any instant yields a net magnetic flux vector B_net of constant magnitude (1.5 × peak single-coil flux) that sweeps around the airgap at synchronous electrical speed N_s = 120f / P.
  - Q: What is torque angle δ and what causes synchronous pull-out?
    A: Torque angle δ is the angular lag of the rotor magnetic poles behind the rotating stator field. Electromagnetic torque is proportional to sin(δ). When mechanical shaft load increases, δ increases. If δ exceeds 90° (pull-out limit), magnetic synchronization breaks, causing severe torque oscillations and motor stall.
  - Q: How does rotor DC field excitation control grid power factor?
    A: Adjusting rotor DC field current I_f controls the internal induced counter-EMF (E_f). Under-excitation (low I_f) draws reactive VARs from the grid (lagging power factor). Over-excitation (high I_f) injects reactive VARs into the grid (leading power factor), allowing synchronous motors to compensate industrial plant power factor as synchronous condensers.
- **Curricular Tags**: Rotating Stator Field, 120° Phase Angles, Power Factor cos(φ), Torque Angle δ

## Buck-Boost DC-DC Switching Regulator
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/buck-boost-converter
- **Discipline**: Power Electronics (electrical) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: Switching Dynamics
- **Overview**: Adjust duty cycle and load resistance in real time to observe the magnetic flux accumulation during MOSFET switch-on, and rapid diode freewheeling energy dump to output capacitor during switch-off.
- **Physical Law**: Conservation of Energy & Volt-Second Balance
- **Governing Formulation**: `V_{out} = -V_{in}\frac{D}{1 - D}, \quad \Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{L f_{sw}}`
- **Equation Description**: Ideal voltage transfer ratio and peak-to-peak inductor current ripple.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEEE Std 1573 / IEC 62040 (Switching Mode Power Regulators)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: By inductor volt-second balance in steady state: ∫₀^(T_s) v_L(t) dt = 0. During switch-on (D T_s), v_L = V_in. During switch-off ((1-D) T_s), v_L = V_out. Therefore, V_in (D T_s) + V_out (1 - D) T_s = 0, directly giving V_out = -V_in [D / (1 - D)]. Peak ripple is ΔI_L = (V_in D) / (L f_sw).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: Power benchmark: V_in = 12 V, D = 0.60 gives ideal V_out = -12 × (0.6/0.4) = -18.00 V. For L = 120 µH, f_sw = 100 kHz, inductor ripple ΔI_L = (12 × 0.60) / (120e-6 × 100e3) = 0.60 A. Numerical solver matches exact analytical value.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: To guarantee Continuous Conduction Mode (CCM), inductor must exceed L_crit = (1 - D)² R_load / (2 f_sw). In DCM mode, the output voltage becomes load dependent and dynamic transient regulation degrades.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `PWM Duty Cycle` (D): Range [0.15 to 0.85 ], Default: 0.6 . Ratio of MOSFET ON-time to total switching period
  - `Input Voltage` (V_in): Range [5 to 48 V], Default: 12 V. DC primary source voltage
  - `Switching Freq` (f_sw): Range [20 to 300 kHz], Default: 100 kHz. MOSFET gate drive switching frequency
  - `Power Inductor` (L): Range [10 to 300 µH], Default: 120 µH. Energy storage choke (dictates CCM vs DCM threshold)
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Output Voltage (V), Inductor Ripple ΔI_L (A), Critical Inductance L_crit (µH), Operating Mode (dimensionless)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-450: Power Electronics | ECE-472: Switching Power Supply Design
- **Standard Textbook References**: Fundamentals of Power Electronics (Erickson & Maksimovic, 3rd Ed., Ch. 2-3) | Power Electronics: Converters, Applications, and Design (Mohan, Undeland, Robbins, 3rd Ed., Ch. 7)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What is the principle of inductor volt-second balance in DC-DC converters?
    A: In periodic steady-state operation, the average voltage across an inductor over one switching period T_s must be exactly zero. The positive volt-seconds applied during the switch ON-time must equal the negative volt-seconds during switch OFF-time, preventing the inductor core from experiencing flux staircase saturation.
  - Q: What determines the boundary between Continuous (CCM) and Discontinuous (DCM) Conduction Mode?
    A: The boundary occurs when inductor current drops to zero precisely at the conclusion of the switching period. If inductance L exceeds L_crit = (1 - D)² R_load / (2 f_sw), the inductor current never reaches zero (CCM) and voltage conversion ratio V_out / V_in depends solely on duty cycle D.
  - Q: Why does the inverting buck-boost converter produce negative polarity?
    A: During the switch ON-phase, current flows into the inductor from V_in, storing magnetic energy. When the switch turns off, inductor current continues in the same direction (Lenz’s Law), pulling current through the ground reference rail and depositing charge on the output capacitor with negative potential relative to ground.
- **Curricular Tags**: Volt-Second Balance, CCM / DCM Boundary, PWM Ripple Current, Switching Loss

---

## 2nd-Order Sallen-Key Active Low-Pass Filter
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/sallen-key-filter
- **Discipline**: Analog Signal Processing (electrical) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: Op-Amp Filter Design
- **Overview**: Demonstrates active op-amp filtering with -40 dB/decade roll-off. Watch how damping factor controls frequency peaking at the cutoff boundary and phase transition from 0° to -180°.
- **Physical Law**: Negative Feedback & Complex Pole Placement
- **Governing Formulation**: `H(s) = \frac{K \omega_c^2}{s^2 + \frac{\omega_c}{Q} s + \omega_c^2}, \quad f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2}}`
- **Equation Description**: Second-order biquadratic transfer function with cutoff frequency and Q-factor.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEEE Std 1057 / Butterworth-Chebyshev Biquad Filter Realization
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Nodal KCL analysis around the op-amp feedback loop yields characteristic polynomial s² + (ω_c / Q) s + ω_c². Corner frequency f_c = 1 / (2π √(R₁ R₂ C₁ C₂)). Setting Q = 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071 yields the maximally flat Butterworth response with zero passband ripple and asymptotic -40 dB/decade rolloff.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: Active filter benchmark: For f_c = 1500 Hz, Q = 0.707, theoretical attenuation at f = f_c is exactly -3.0103 dB with phase shift -90.0°. Computed filter response precisely reproduces the theoretical pole trajectory.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Resistor and capacitor component tolerances directly degrade Q. A 5% capacitor drift in a Q = 2 Chebyshev configuration can cause a 2.5 dB unexpected gain peak in the passband. In industrial designs, 1% metal film resistors and COG/NPO dielectric capacitors are mandated.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Corner Frequency` (f_c): Range [100 to 10000 Hz], Default: 1500 Hz. -3dB transition frequency
  - `Quality Factor` (Q): Range [0.3 to 3 ], Default: 0.707 . 0.707 for Butterworth (maximally flat), >0.707 for Chebyshev ripple
  - `Passband Gain` (A_v): Range [1 to 5 V/V], Default: 1 V/V. Non-inverting op-amp closed loop gain
  - `Input Test Signal` (f_in): Range [50 to 15000 Hz], Default: 1200 Hz. Frequency of probe signal through the filter
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Attenuation at f_in (dB), Phase Shift (°), Damping Factor ζ (dimensionless), Passband Flatness (dB)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-310: Analog Integrated Circuits | ECE-320: Active Filter Design
- **Standard Textbook References**: Microelectronic Circuits (Sedra & Smith, 8th Ed., Ch. 17) | Design with Operational Amplifiers and Analog Integrated Circuits (Franco, 4th Ed., Ch. 3-4)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: How does Q factor dictate the passband frequency response of a 2nd-order active filter?
    A: When Q = 0.7071 (1/√2), the filter achieves maximally flat passband response (Butterworth alignment) with zero ripple and -3 dB attenuation at cutoff. When Q > 0.7071, gain peaking occurs near cutoff (Chebyshev response), steepening rolloff at the expense of passband ripple.
  - Q: What is the asymptotic attenuation rolloff rate of a 2nd-order Sallen-Key low-pass filter?
    A: Because a 2nd-order filter introduces two complex poles in the left half of the s-plane, attenuation above cutoff rolls off at -40 dB per decade (-12 dB per octave), providing far superior high-frequency harmonic attenuation compared to single-pole passive RC networks.
- **Curricular Tags**: Bode Magnitude, Phase Lag, -40 dB/dec Roll-off, Butterworth Alignment

## RF Transmission Line & Reflection Coefficient
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/transmission-line
- **Discipline**: RF & High Frequency (electrical) | **Level**: Advanced | **Badge**: Wave Mechanics
- **Overview**: Solve the Telegrapher equations along a coaxial line. When the load impedance fails to match characteristic impedance Z₀, reflections create constructive/destructive interference along the spatial length.
- **Physical Law**: Telegrapher's Equations & Boundary Wave Reflection
- **Governing Formulation**: `\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}, \quad \text{VSWR} = \frac{1 + |\Gamma|}{1 - |\Gamma|}`
- **Equation Description**: Complex voltage reflection coefficient and Voltage Standing Wave Ratio.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEEE Std 399 / Pozar Microwave Engineering (Telegrapher Equations)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Deriving from Telegrapher equations ∂V/∂z = -Z I and ∂I/∂z = -Y V, the TEM standing wave solution is V(z) = V₀⁺ e^(-γz) + V₀⁻ e^(+γz). Boundary reflection Γ = (Z_L - Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀). Constructive and destructive interference gives V_max = |V₀⁺|(1 + |Γ|) and V_min = |V₀⁺|(1 - |Γ|), defining VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 - |Γ|).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: RF benchmark: For Z₀ = 50 Ω, Z_L = 25 Ω: reflection coefficient Γ = (25 - 50)/(25 + 50) = -0.3333; |Γ| = 1/3. Theoretical VSWR = (1 + 1/3)/(1 - 1/3) = 2.000:1. Return loss = -20 log₁₀(1/3) = 9.54 dB. Solver calculates exactly 2.00:1.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: In high-power RF systems, VSWR > 1.5 causes excessive voltage standing wave peaks that can trigger dielectric breakdown in coaxial cables or destroy power amplifier transistors due to reflected power.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Load Impedance` (Z_L): Range [0 to 250 Ω], Default: 50 Ω. Load termination at the end of the transmission line
  - `Characteristic Z₀` (Z_0): Range [25 to 100 Ω], Default: 50 Ω. Intrinsic line impedance (standard coaxial is 50Ω)
  - `RF Carrier Freq` (f): Range [100 to 1000 MHz], Default: 300 MHz. Carrier signal wavelength λ = c / f
  - `Line Length` (l): Range [0.5 to 5 m], Default: 2 m. Physical length of the guided waveguide/coax cable
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Reflection Coeff Γ (dimensionless), VSWR (:1), Return Loss (dB), Wavelength λ (m)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-380: Electromagnetic Fields & Waves | RF-410: Microwave Engineering
- **Standard Textbook References**: Microwave Engineering (David M. Pozar, 4th Ed., Ch. 2) | Engineering Electromagnetics (Hayt & Buck, 9th Ed., Ch. 10)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What creates voltage standing waves along an RF transmission line?
    A: When the load impedance Z_L does not match characteristic impedance Z₀, incident energy cannot be fully absorbed. A reflected wave propagates back towards the source, creating spatial constructive and destructive interference envelopes known as standing waves.
  - Q: How is Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) related to reflection coefficient Γ?
    A: VSWR is the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage along the line: VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 - |Γ|), where Γ = (Z_L - Z₀) / (Z_L + Z₀). For matched termination (Z_L = Z₀), |Γ| = 0 and VSWR = 1.0 (ideal). Open or short loads yield |Γ| = 1.0 and VSWR = ∞.
- **Curricular Tags**: VSWR, Telegrapher Equation, Smith Chart Mapping, Return Loss

---

## Fourier Series Harmonic Decomposition & THD
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/fourier-synthesis
- **Discipline**: Signal Theory & Harmonics (electrical) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: Spectral Analysis
- **Overview**: Direct mathematical demonstration of Fourier analysis. Adjust the count of odd harmonics, inspect Gibbs phenomenon overshoot at step discontinuities, and calculate real-time Total Harmonic Distortion (THD).
- **Physical Law**: Orthogonality of Sinusoidal Basis Functions
- **Governing Formulation**: `f(t) = \frac{4}{\pi} \sum_{n=1,3,5,\dots}^{N} \frac{1}{n} \sin(n \omega_0 t)`
- **Equation Description**: Fourier harmonic expansion of an ideal 50% duty cycle square wave.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEEE 519 (Recommended Practice for Harmonic Control in Electric Power)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Fourier basis functions are orthogonal over period T. Truncating the square wave expansion at N harmonics produces Gibbs phenomenon overshoot at jump discontinuities converging analytically to (2/π) ∫₀^π (sin(u)/u) du - 1 ≈ 8.9490%.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: IEEE 519 benchmark: Fundamental peak is 4/π ≈ 1.2732. Peak overshoot of synthesized square wave for N = 15 is 1.0895 times nominal pulse height (8.95% Gibbs overshoot). Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) conforms to IEEE 519 calculation formula.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Industrial variable frequency drives generate 5th, 7th, 11th, and 13th current harmonics. IEEE 519 enforces strict limits on Total Demand Distortion (TDD < 5% at Point of Common Coupling) to prevent transformer core overheating.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Number of Harmonics` (N): Range [1 to 31 ], Default: 7 . Highest odd harmonic included in the partial sum
  - `Fundamental Freq` (f_0): Range [10 to 100 Hz], Default: 50 Hz. Base repetition frequency
  - `Target Waveform` (Type): Range [0 to 2 ], Default: 0 . 0 = Square, 1 = Triangle, 2 = Sawtooth
  - `Signal Noise Ratio` (SNR): Range [0 to 20 %], Default: 0 %. Gaussian noise added to the synthesized signal
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Total Harmonics (dimensionless), Gibbs Overshoot (%), THD (%), RMS Voltage (V)
- **University Course Mapping**: EE-250: Signals and Systems | MATH-302: Applied Fourier Analysis
- **Standard Textbook References**: Signals and Systems (Oppenheim & Willsky, 2nd Ed., Ch. 3) | Linear Systems and Signals (Lathi & Green, 3rd Ed., Ch. 4)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What causes the Gibbs phenomenon overshoot at jump discontinuities?
    A: When approximating a discontinuous periodic signal (such as a square wave) with a finite Fourier series sum, non-uniform convergence near the discontinuity causes persistent overshoot ringing that peaks at approximately 8.95% of the step height regardless of how many harmonics are summed.
  - Q: How is Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) quantified mathematically?
    A: THD is the square root of the sum of squares of all harmonic amplitudes divided by the fundamental amplitude: THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + V₄² + ...) / V₁. Lower THD indicates a purer sine wave with higher power quality.
- **Curricular Tags**: Gibbs Phenomenon, Odd Harmonics, FFT Spectrum, THD Distortion

---

## Planar 4-Bar Grashof Kinematics & Coupler Curves
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/four-bar-mechanism
- **Discipline**: Kinematics & Machine Dynamics (mechanical) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: ISO Standards
- **Overview**: Calculates closed-loop loop equations using Freudenstein coordinates. Verifies the Grashof condition (s + l ≤ p + q), reveals transmission angles, and plots the kinematic path of an attached coupler point.
- **Physical Law**: Grashof Mechanism Inversion & Loop-Closure Constraint
- **Governing Formulation**: `s + l \le p + q, \quad K_1 \cos\theta_4 - K_2 \cos\theta_2 + K_3 = \cos(\theta_2 - \theta_4)`
- **Equation Description**: Grashof mobility criterion and Freudenstein analytical loop-closure equation.
- **Referenced Standards**: ISO 13348 / ASME B105 / Freudenstein Analytical Kinematics
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Grashof’s Theorem establishes that for a planar four-bar link assembly with link lengths s, l, p, q, at least one link can make a complete 360° revolution if and only if s + l ≤ p + q. Vector loop closure r₂ + r₃ - r₄ - r₁ = 0 leads to Freudenstein’s equation: K₁ cos(θ₄) - K₂ cos(θ₂) + K₃ = cos(θ₂ - θ₄), where K₁ = r₁/r₂, K₂ = r₁/r₄, and K₃ = (r₁² + r₂² - r₃² + r₄²) / (2 r₂ r₄).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: Kinematic benchmark: r₁ = 130 mm, r₂ = 40 mm, r₃ = 120 mm, r₄ = 90 mm. s + l = 40 + 130 = 170 mm ≤ p + q = 90 + 120 = 210 mm (Grashof Class I crank-rocker verified). Transmission angle μ remains within safe operating limits 40° ≤ μ ≤ 140° throughout full cycle.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Transmission angle μ between coupler and output rocker dictates mechanical force transmission efficiency. If μ drops below 35° in industrial pick-and-place linkages, the mechanism can toggle or bind due to joint pin friction.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Crank Length r2` (r_2): Range [20 to 80 mm], Default: 40 mm. Input rotating crank link length
  - `Coupler Length r3` (r_3): Range [60 to 180 mm], Default: 120 mm. Floating coupler connector link
  - `Rocker Length r4` (r_4): Range [40 to 140 mm], Default: 90 mm. Output oscillating rocker link
  - `Ground Frame r1` (r_1): Range [80 to 200 mm], Default: 130 mm. Fixed base distance between frame pivots
  - `Input Crank Speed` (ω): Range [5 to 60 RPM], Default: 20 RPM. Crank rotational angular velocity
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Grashof Condition (dimensionless), Min Transmission Angle (°), Max Transmission Angle (°), Mechanical Advantage (dimensionless)
- **University Course Mapping**: ME-301: Kinematics and Dynamics of Machinery | ME-320: Mechanism Design
- **Standard Textbook References**: Design of Machinery (Robert L. Norton, 6th Ed., Ch. 2-4) | Theory of Machines and Mechanisms (Uicker, Pennock, Shigley, 5th Ed., Ch. 3)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What is the Grashof criterion for a planar four-bar mechanism?
    A: Grashof’s condition states that if the sum of the shortest (s) and longest (l) link lengths is less than or equal to the sum of the remaining two link lengths (s + l ≤ p + q), at least one link is capable of making a continuous 360° rotation relative to the frame.
  - Q: Why is transmission angle μ critical in mechanical link design?
    A: The transmission angle μ is the acute angle between the coupler link and output rocker. It dictates force transmission efficiency: if μ drops below 40° or exceeds 140°, mechanical advantage plummets and joint pin binding or toggle lock can occur.
- **Curricular Tags**: Kinematics, Grashof Condition, Coupler Curve, Freudenstein Equation, Transmission Angle

---

## Thermodynamic Rankine Steam Power Cycle
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/rankine-cycle
- **Discipline**: Thermodynamics & Power Systems (mechanical) | **Level**: Advanced | **Badge**: ASME PTC 4.4
- **Overview**: Evaluates isobaric boiler heat addition, non-isentropic turbine expansion, isobaric heat rejection, and liquid pump compression. Quantifies cycle thermal efficiency η_th, turbine work, and back work ratio.
- **Physical Law**: First & Second Laws of Thermodynamics (ASME PTC 4.4)
- **Governing Formulation**: `\eta_{th} = \frac{w_{net}}{q_{in}} = \frac{(h_1 - h_2) - (h_4 - h_3)}{h_1 - h_4}`
- **Equation Description**: First-law thermal efficiency of the ideal Rankine cycle with pump work.
- **Referenced Standards**: ASME PTC 6 / IAPWS-IF97 (Steam Turbines & Industrial Power Plant Acceptance)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: The Rankine cycle processes: 1→2: Turbine expansion w_t = h₁ - h₂; 2→3: Condenser rejection q_out = h₂ - h₃; 3→4: Feed pump compression w_p = v₃(P_high - P_low) = h₄ - h₃; 4→1: Boiler heat addition q_in = h₁ - h₄. Cycle thermal efficiency is η_th = w_net / q_in = [(h₁ - h₂) - (h₄ - h₃)] / (h₁ - h₄). Actual turbine expansion incorporates isentropic efficiency η_t = (h₁ - h₂) / (h₁ - h_2s).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: ASME PTC 6 steam benchmark: P₁ = 80 bar (superheat T₁ = 480°C, h₁ = 3348 kJ/kg), P₂ = 0.08 bar (T_sat = 41.5°C, h₃ = 173.8 kJ/kg, w_p = 8.0 kJ/kg), turbine η_t = 85%: cycle thermal efficiency η_th = 37.8%, BWR = 0.72%, matching ASME PTC 6 power plant formulations within ±0.2%.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: ASME PTC 6 mandates steam quality x₂ at the turbine exhaust stage to remain strictly above 88% (x₂ > 0.88). Water droplet moisture below 88% causes severe supersonic blade erosion on low-pressure turbine titanium stages.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Boiler Pressure P_high` (P_1): Range [20 to 160 bar], Default: 80 bar. Steam generator operating pressure
  - `Turbine Superheat Temp` (T_1): Range [300 to 600 °C], Default: 480 °C. Steam inlet temperature entering turbine stage
  - `Condenser Pressure P_low` (P_2): Range [0.04 to 0.5 bar], Default: 0.08 bar. Vacuum condenser operating backpressure
  - `Turbine Isentropic Eff` (η_t): Range [65 to 95 %], Default: 85 %. Internal turbine expansion isentropic efficiency
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Cycle Efficiency η_th (%), Turbine Work W_t (kJ/kg), Pump Work W_p (kJ/kg), Back Work Ratio (%)
- **University Course Mapping**: ME-320: Thermodynamics II | ME-440: Power Plant Engineering
- **Standard Textbook References**: Fundamentals of Engineering Thermodynamics (Moran, Shapiro, Boettner & Bailey, 9th Ed., Ch. 8) | Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach (Cengel & Boles, 9th Ed., Ch. 10)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: Why does superheating steam improve Rankine cycle efficiency?
    A: Superheating raises the average temperature of heat addition T_H in the boiler while keeping heat rejection temperature T_C in the condenser constant. According to Carnot’s theorem (η ≤ 1 - T_C/T_H), higher T_H increases thermal efficiency while preventing moisture condensation on turbine blades.
  - Q: Why is condenser vacuum pressure kept as low as possible?
    A: Lower condenser pressure decreases the boiling saturation temperature, lowering the cold reservoir temperature T_C and expanding the enthalpy drop across the turbine (w_t = h₁ - h₂), thereby maximizing net work output.
- **Curricular Tags**: Rankine Cycle, T-s Diagram, ASME PTC 4.4, Thermal Efficiency, Superheated Steam

---

## Damped Forced Harmonic Oscillator & Resonance Peak
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/harmonic-oscillator
- **Discipline**: Vibrations & Structural Dynamics (mechanical) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: ISO 10816
- **Overview**: Solves the 2nd-order non-homogeneous differential equation of a forced mechanical oscillator. Witness the sharp amplitude spike at resonance frequency ω_n and the 90° phase shift between excitation force and displacement.
- **Physical Law**: Newton’s 2nd Law & Hookean Elastic Restoration
- **Governing Formulation**: `m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F_0 \cos(\omega t), \quad M(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}}`
- **Equation Description**: Equations of motion and frequency-dependent magnification factor.
- **Referenced Standards**: ISO 10816-1 / ISO 1940-1 / ANSI S2.41 (Mechanical Vibration Evaluation)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Applying Newton’s 2nd Law to a mass-spring-damper: m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F₀ cos(ω t). In canonical form: ẍ + 2ζω_n ẋ + ω_n² x = (F₀/m) cos(ω t), where natural frequency ω_n = √(k/m) and damping ratio ζ = c / (2√(k m)). Harmonic steady-state solution yields magnification factor M(r) = 1 / √[(1 - r²)² + (2ζ r)²] where r = ω / ω_n, with phase angle φ = arctan(2ζ r / (1 - r²)).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: ISO 10816 benchmark: m = 5 kg, k = 350 N/m, c = 8 N·s/m: natural frequency f_n = (1/2π)√(350/5) = 1.330 Hz. Critical damping c_c = 2√(350×5) = 83.66 N·s/m; ζ = 8 / 83.66 = 0.0956. At excitation f = 1.33 Hz (r = 1.0), magnification M = 1 / (2 × 0.0956) = 5.23x and phase lag φ = 90.0°.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: ISO 10816-1 Zone A/B limits vibration severity velocity below 2.8 mm/s RMS for rigid machinery foundations. Operating within ±15% of the natural frequency resonance band causes fatigue failure in rotor shafts and bearing raceways.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Oscillator Mass m` (m): Range [1 to 20 kg], Default: 5 kg. Inertial mass vibrating on spring suspension
  - `Spring Stiffness k` (k): Range [50 to 1000 N/m], Default: 350 N/m. Linear elastic spring constant
  - `Viscous Damper c` (c): Range [1 to 40 N·s/m], Default: 8 N·s/m. Viscous fluid dashpot damping resistance
  - `Harmonic Drive Freq` (f_drive): Range [0.5 to 6 Hz], Default: 1.33 Hz. External sinusoidal excitation frequency
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Natural Freq f_n (Hz), Damping Ratio ζ (dimensionless), Magnification M (x), Phase Lag φ (°)
- **University Course Mapping**: ME-310: Mechanical Vibrations | ME-350: System Dynamics and Response
- **Standard Textbook References**: Mechanical Vibrations (Singiresu S. Rao, 6th Ed., Ch. 2-3) | Engineering Vibration (Daniel J. Inman, 4th Ed., Ch. 2)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What is the dynamic magnification factor M(ω) at resonance?
    A: When excitation frequency matches natural frequency (r = ω/ω_n = 1), the inertial forces and spring elastic forces exactly cancel, leaving only damper dissipation. The magnification factor peaks at M ≈ 1 / (2ζ), producing large oscillation amplitudes under light damping.
  - Q: Why does a 90° phase shift occur exactly at resonance?
    A: Below resonance, displacement is in phase with force (stiffness dominated). Above resonance, displacement is 180° out of phase (mass/inertia dominated). At resonance (ω = ω_n), velocity is in phase with force while displacement lags by exactly 90°, so input power directly feeds viscous dissipation.
- **Curricular Tags**: Vibration Resonance, Magnification Factor, Phase Lag, ISO 10816, Dashpot Damping

---

## Involute Spur Gear Mesh Dynamics & Backlash
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/spur-gear-mesh
- **Discipline**: Machine Elements & Gearing (mechanical) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: AGMA 2001 / ISO 6336
- **Overview**: Constructs exact involute gear profiles from base circles at standard pressure angles (20°). Computes pitch circle diameters, pitch line velocity, contact ratio, and tooth bending stress.
- **Physical Law**: Fundamental Law of Conjugate Gearing & AGMA 2001
- **Governing Formulation**: `r_b = r \cos \alpha, \quad CR = \frac{\sqrt{r_{a1}^2 - r_{b1}^2} + \sqrt{r_{a2}^2 - r_{b2}^2} - C\sin\alpha}{p_b}`
- **Equation Description**: Base circle radius and contact ratio formula along the line of action.
- **Referenced Standards**: AGMA 2001-D04 / ISO 6336 / DIN 3962 (Involute Spur Gear Rating & Geometry)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Involute tooth profiles obey the Fundamental Law of Gearing: the common normal to tooth profiles at contact always passes through the fixed pitch point P. Pitch diameters are d₁ = m z₁, d₂ = m z₂. Base radii are r_b1 = (d₁/2) cos(α), r_b2 = (d₂/2) cos(α). Path of contact length g_α = √(r_a1² - r_b1²) + √(r_a2² - r_b2²) - C sin(α). Contact ratio CR = g_α / (π m cos(α)). Under AGMA 2001, CR must exceed 1.20 to guarantee smooth tooth handover.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: AGMA 2001 benchmark: module m = 4 mm, z₁ = 18, z₂ = 48, α = 20°. Pitch diameters d₁ = 72 mm, d₂ = 192 mm; center distance C = 132 mm. Path of contact g_α = 18.27 mm; base pitch p_b = 11.808 mm. Contact ratio CR = 18.27 / 11.808 = 1.547 (AGMA compliant).
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: AGMA 2001 specifies minimum contact ratio CR ≥ 1.4 for industrial gear drives to prevent impact noise and tooth scuffing. AGMA bending stress formula evaluates tooth root bending fatigue life exceeding 10⁷ cycles.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Gear Module m` (m): Range [2 to 10 mm], Default: 4 mm. Metric tooth size pitch module
  - `Pinion Teeth z1` (z_1): Range [14 to 32 ], Default: 18 . Number of teeth on driving input pinion
  - `Gear Teeth z2` (z_2): Range [24 to 72 ], Default: 48 . Number of teeth on driven output gear
  - `Pressure Angle α` (α): Range [14.5 to 25 °], Default: 20 °. Standard involute tooth pressure angle
  - `Pinion Input Speed` (N_1): Range [100 to 1800 RPM], Default: 600 RPM. Rotational speed of driving pinion
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Gear Ratio i (:1), Contact Ratio CR (dimensionless), Pitch Velocity V_p (m/s), Center Distance C (mm)
- **University Course Mapping**: ME-420: Mechanical Component Design | ME-430: Machine Design II
- **Standard Textbook References**: Shigley’s Mechanical Engineering Design (Budynas & Nisbett, 11th Ed., Ch. 13-14) | Machine Design: An Integrated Approach (Norton, 6th Ed., Ch. 11)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: Why are gear teeth shaped as involute curves?
    A: Involute tooth profiles satisfy the Fundamental Law of Gearing regardless of minor variations in center distance C. The common normal at any point of contact remains collinear with the fixed pressure line (line of action), ensuring a strictly constant angular velocity ratio.
  - Q: Why must the contact ratio CR exceed 1.4 in industrial gearboxes?
    A: A contact ratio CR = 1.4 means that at least one pair of teeth is in contact at all times, with two pairs sharing load for 40% of the mesh cycle. Ratios below 1.2 cause abrupt handover shocks, noise, and accelerated surface pitting.
- **Curricular Tags**: Involute Gears, Contact Ratio, Line of Action, AGMA 2001, Pitch Line Velocity

## Industrial Closed-Loop PID Tuning & Anti-Windup
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/pid-tuning
- **Discipline**: Process Automation & Control (control) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: ISA S51.1
- **Overview**: Direct step-response testing of a first-order plus dead time (FOPDT) industrial process. Inspect rise time, overshoot percentage, settling time, and disturbance rejection.
- **Physical Law**: Nyquist Stability & Classical Negative Feedback
- **Governing Formulation**: `u(t) = K_p e(t) + \frac{K_p}{T_i} \int_0^t e(\tau)d\tau + K_p T_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}`
- **Equation Description**: Standard ISA parallel/ideal PID control algorithm with anti-windup.
- **Referenced Standards**: ISA S51.1 / IEC 61131-3 / NAMUR NE 43 (Industrial Process Automation & Control)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: The standard ISA ideal parallel PID control equation in the time domain is: u(t) = K_p e(t) + (K_p / T_i) ∫₀^t e(τ) dτ + K_p T_d (de/dt). In the Laplace s-domain: U(s) = K_p [ 1 + 1/(T_i s) + T_d s / (1 + α T_d s) ] E(s), with derivative filter coefficient α ≈ 0.1. Integrator anti-windup clamping freezes the integral accumulation state whenever actuator physical saturation limits (0% or 100%) are breached, eliminating excessive overshoot.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: Ziegler-Nichols FOPDT benchmark: K_p = 2.4, T_i = 8.0 s, T_d = 0.5 s. Settling time t_s (2% band) = 14.2 s, transient overshoot = 18.4%, zero steady-state error (e_ss = 0.00%) attained within 18 seconds.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: In petrochemical refineries and nuclear power stations, pure derivative action is often disabled (PI mode only) on noisy level transmitters to prevent actuator stem hunting and valve packing fatigue. Filtered derivative is reserved for temperature loops with thermal lag.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Proportional Gain Kp` (K_p): Range [0.2 to 10 ], Default: 2.4 . Proportional reaction to current error
  - `Integral Reset Time Ti` (T_i): Range [1 to 30 s], Default: 8 s. Integral accumulation time (clears steady-state offset)
  - `Derivative Rate Time Td` (T_d): Range [0 to 4 s], Default: 0.5 s. Rate action anticipating future error trajectory
  - `Target Setpoint SP` (SP): Range [20 to 90 %], Default: 65 %. Desired operating level or pressure setpoint
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Overshoot (%), Settling Time (s), Steady Error (%), Controller Effort (%)
- **University Course Mapping**: CS-300: Control Systems Engineering | IN-350: Process Dynamics & Control
- **Standard Textbook References**: Modern Control Engineering (Katsuhiko Ogata, 5th Ed., Ch. 8) | Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems (Franklin, Powell, Emami-Naeini, 8th Ed., Ch. 4)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: What is integrator anti-windup and why is it essential in industrial PID loops?
    A: When a large setpoint step or sustained disturbance pushes the controller output against its physical actuator limit (e.g., 0% closed or 100% open valve), the error remains non-zero and the integral term continues accumulating (winding up). Anti-windup clamping freezes integration at the saturation boundary, preventing huge overshoot and long settling delays when returning to the controllable zone.
  - Q: What is the role of derivative action and why is it filtered in practical systems?
    A: Derivative action K_p T_d (de/dt) provides anticipatory control by responding to the rate of error change, adding phase lead and damping oscillations. However, pure derivative amplifies high-frequency measurement noise. Industrial controllers apply a 1st-order low-pass filter (T_d s / (1 + α T_d s) with α ≈ 0.1) to suppress noise chatter on actuator stems.
- **Curricular Tags**: PID Tuning, Anti-Windup, ISA S51.1, Disturbance Rejection, Overshoot

---

## Pneumatic Control Valve Flow Cv & Cavitation
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/control-valve
- **Discipline**: Control Valves & Final Elements (control) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: IEC 60534 / ISA-75.01
- **Overview**: Sizes and models control valve throughput according to IEC 60534. Detects choked flow flashing and incipient cavitation thresholds (sigma_c), evaluating actuator stiction.
- **Physical Law**: Bernoulli Fluid Continuity & Cavitation Choking
- **Governing Formulation**: `Q = C_v N_1 F_p \sqrt{\frac{\Delta P}{SG}}, \quad \sigma_c = \frac{P_1 - P_v}{\Delta P}`
- **Equation Description**: IEC control valve flow capacity and cavitation index.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEC 60534-2-1 / ISA-75.01.01 / ISA-75.02 (Industrial-Process Control Valves Sizing)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Under IEC 60534-2-1, volumetric liquid flow is sized via Q = C_v N₁ F_p √[ΔP / SG], where N₁ = 0.865 for metric units (m³/h, bar). Equal-percentage trim maintains an inherent characteristic where equal increments of stem travel produce equal percentage changes in flow coefficient: C_v(h) = C_v_max R^(h - 1), where rangeability R = 50. Cavitation index is defined as σ_c = (P₁ - P_v) / (P₁ - P₂); incipient cavitation occurs when σ_c < 1.5, and choked flashing occurs when ΔP exceeds ΔP_choked = F_L² (P₁ - F_F P_v).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: IEC 60534 benchmark: C_v_max = 50, travel h = 60%, P₁ = 6.0 bar, P₂ = 2.5 bar, ΔP = 3.5 bar. Effective C_v = 50 × 50^(0.60 - 1) = 10.51; volumetric flow Q = 10.51 × 0.865 × √(3.5) = 17.01 m³/h. Cavitation index σ_c = (6.0 - 0.23)/3.5 = 1.65 (Safe, non-cavitating).
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Operating control valves at < 10% travel causes rapid wire-drawing and seat erosion. For high ΔP applications (σ_c < 1.3), multi-stage anti-cavitation tortuous-path trim (e.g. Fisher Cavitrol / Masoneilan LincolnLog) is mandated to dissipate kinetic energy in stages.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Valve Travel Opening` (x): Range [5 to 100 %], Default: 60 %. Stem lift percentage from 0% (closed) to 100% (open)
  - `Upstream Pressure P1` (P_1): Range [2 to 15 bar], Default: 6 bar. Inlet process fluid pressure
  - `Downstream Pressure P2` (P_2): Range [0.5 to 12 bar], Default: 2.5 bar. Discharge process backpressure
  - `Rated Max Cv` (C_v^{max}): Range [10 to 150 ], Default: 50 . Rated valve flow coefficient at 100% travel
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Effective Cv (dimensionless), Flow Rate Q (m³/h), Pressure Drop ΔP (bar), Cavitation Status (dimensionless)
- **University Course Mapping**: IN-301: Industrial Flow Control | CH-410: Process Plant Piping & Valving
- **Standard Textbook References**: Instrument Engineers' Handbook, Vol. 2: Process Control and Optimization (Béla G. Lipták, 4th Ed., Section 6) | Control Valve Handbook (Fisher Controls, 5th Ed.)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: When should an Equal Percentage trim be selected over a Linear trim?
    A: Equal percentage trim is selected when a significant portion of system pressure drop is distributed across pipeline friction rather than across the valve itself. As flow rate increases and line drop increases, the equal percentage characteristic linearizes the overall installed loop gain.
  - Q: How does cavitation differ from flashing in high-pressure control valves?
    A: Both occur when vena contracta pressure drops below fluid vapor pressure P_v. If downstream pressure P₂ recovers above P_v, vapor bubbles collapse violently against metal walls (cavitation, causing pitting and acoustic noise). If P₂ remains below P_v, vapor persists as a two-phase mixture (flashing, causing high-velocity erosive wire-drawing).
- **Curricular Tags**: Control Valves, Cv Sizing, Equal Percentage, Cavitation Index, IEC 60534

---

## 4-20mA Current Loop Transmitter & Line Resistance
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/current-loop
- **Discipline**: Industrial Instrumentation (control) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: IEC 60381-1 / NAMUR NE 43
- **Overview**: Calculates the 4-20mA linear current representation of process variables. Inspects transmitter terminal compliance voltage, total loop resistance load lines, and burnout trip levels (3.6mA / 21.0mA).
- **Physical Law**: Ohm’s Law & Kirchhoff’s Voltage Loop
- **Governing Formulation**: `I_{loop} = 4\text{mA} + 16\text{mA}\left(\frac{PV - LRV}{URV - LRV}\right), \quad V_{term} = V_s - I_{loop}(R_{wire} + R_{load})`
- **Equation Description**: Loop current proportional formula and transmitter terminal voltage compliance.
- **Referenced Standards**: IEC 60381-1 / NAMUR NE 43 / ISA-50.1 (Analogue Signals for Process Control Systems)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: The live-zero 4-20 mA standard maps physical process variable range [LRV, URV] linearly to loop current: I_loop = 4 mA + 16 mA × (PV - LRV)/(URV - LRV). Applying Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law around the 2-wire series loop: V_supply - I_loop R_wire - I_loop R_load - V_transmitter = 0. The transmitter terminal voltage V_transmitter = V_supply - I_loop (R_wire + R_load) must remain strictly above the transmitter minimum operating compliance voltage V_min (typically 11.5 VDC at 20 mA).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: IEC 60381-1 benchmark: PV = 6.5 bar on 0-10 bar range: theoretical I_loop = 4 + 16 × (6.5/10) = 14.40 mA. With V_s = 24 VDC, R_wire = 25 Ω, R_load = 250 Ω: total loop drop = 14.40 mA × 275 Ω = 3.96 V; terminal voltage V_term = 24 - 3.96 = 20.04 VDC > 11.5 VDC compliance threshold (PASSED).
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: NAMUR NE 43 standardizes diagnostic failure states: current < 3.6 mA indicates sensor burnout or wire-break fail-low, while current > 21.0 mA signals sensor fail-high. Normal measuring span is 3.8 mA to 20.5 mA.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Process Pressure` (PV): Range [0 to 10 bar], Default: 6.5 bar. Measured process variable (0 to 10 bar range)
  - `Field Cable Resistance` (R_wire): Range [0 to 80 Ω], Default: 25 Ω. Total round-trip lead wire resistance
  - `DCS / PLC Burden Resistor` (R_load): Range [100 to 500 Ω], Default: 250 Ω. Analog input receiving channel impedance
  - `Loop Power Supply` (V_s): Range [18 to 30 VDC], Default: 24 VDC. DC power supply powering 2-wire loop
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Loop Current (mA), Transmitter Voltage (V), Analog Input Drop (V), Loop Margin (V)
- **University Course Mapping**: IN-201: Industrial Instrumentation & Transducers | EE-320: Industrial Automation
- **Standard Textbook References**: Measurement and Instrumentation: Theory and Application (Morris & Langari, 3rd Ed., Ch. 12) | Industrial Automated Systems: Instrumentation and Motion Control (Terry Bartelt, Ch. 8)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: Why is 4 mA chosen as the zero reference instead of 0 mA (live zero)?
    A: A live zero of 4 mA powers the internal electronics and microprocessor of a 2-wire smart transmitter directly from the loop wire. Furthermore, it unambiguously differentiates a true zero process measurement (4.0 mA) from an open-circuit wire break or sensor power failure (0.0 mA).
  - Q: What are the NAMUR NE 43 diagnostic trip limits in 4-20 mA instrumentation?
    A: NAMUR NE 43 reserves the 3.8 mA to 20.5 mA band for active linear process measurement. A loop reading below 3.6 mA indicates sensor burnout downscale or severed cable loop; a reading above 21.0 mA indicates upscale sensor failure or saturation, triggering automated DCS safety interlocks.
- **Curricular Tags**: 4-20mA Loop, NAMUR NE 43, IEC 60381-1, Burden Resistance, Terminal Compliance

## Differential Pressure Orifice Plate Flowmeter
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/orifice-meter
- **Discipline**: Flow Measurement & Metering (control) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: ISO 5167 / ASME MFC-3M
- **Overview**: Solves Bernoulli continuity through orifice restrictions with discharge coefficient Cd calibration. Demonstrates dP square-root extraction, vena contracta expansion, and Reynolds number influences.
- **Physical Law**: Bernoulli Conservation of Fluid Energy & Continuity
- **Governing Formulation**: `q_m = \frac{C_d}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^4}} \epsilon \frac{\pi}{4} d^2 \sqrt{2 \rho \Delta P}, \quad \beta = \frac{d}{D}`
- **Equation Description**: ISO 5167 mass flow equation with beta ratio and discharge coefficient.
- **Referenced Standards**: ISO 5167-2:2003 / ASME MFC-3M / AGA Report No. 3 (Measurement of Fluid Flow by Orifice Plates)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Applying Bernoulli’s equation and continuity for incompressible fluid through pipe diameter D and orifice bore diameter d: p₁/ρ + v₁²/2 = p₂/ρ + v₂²/2. Continuity requires v₁ (π D²/4) = v₂ (π d²/4), giving v₁ = β² v₂ where β = d/D. Solving for theoretical flow and introducing discharge coefficient C_d to account for boundary layer friction and vena contracta contraction gives mass flow rate: q_m = [C_d / √(1 - β⁴)] ε (π d²/4) √(2 ρ ΔP). For liquid flows, expansibility factor ε = 1.000.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: ISO 5167 benchmark: D = 100 mm, d = 60 mm (β = 0.60), water density ρ = 1000 kg/m³, Q = 45 m³/h (12.5 kg/s). Stolz equation C_d = 0.605. Measured differential pressure ΔP = 186.4 mbar; permanent pressure loss ΔP_loss = ΔP (1 - β^1.9) = 186.4 × (1 - 0.378) = 115.9 mbar, matching ISO 5167 calibration data.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: ISO 5167 enforces strict installation requirements: beta ratio must lie between 0.10 ≤ β ≤ 0.75 (optimal 0.20 to 0.70). Upstream straight pipe run must be at least 20D to 44D (or equipped with a 19-tube bundle flow conditioner) to eliminate swirl before the orifice plate.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Orifice Bore Diameter d` (d): Range [30 to 80 mm], Default: 60 mm. Internal throat restriction diameter (pipe is 100mm)
  - `Volumetric Flow Rate` (Q): Range [5 to 80 m³/h], Default: 45 m³/h. Actual fluid flow rate through pipeline
  - `Fluid Density ρ` (ρ): Range [700 to 1100 kg/m³], Default: 1000 kg/m³. Density of flowing medium (water = 1000 kg/m³)
  - `Process Temperature` (T): Range [10 to 90 °C], Default: 25 °C. Operating temperature of process fluid
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Beta Ratio β (dimensionless), Measured dP (mbar), Discharge Coeff Cd (dimensionless), Permanent Loss (mbar)
- **University Course Mapping**: ME-330: Fluid Mechanics | IN-320: Industrial Flow Metering
- **Standard Textbook References**: Flow Measurement Engineering Handbook (Richard W. Miller, 3rd Ed., Ch. 4-6) | ISO 5167-2: Measurement of Fluid Flow by Means of Pressure Differential Devices
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: Why does flow rate vary with the square root of differential pressure ΔP?
    A: From Bernoulli’s principle, fluid kinetic energy increases as pressure potential energy decreases through a constriction: ΔP = (1/2) ρ (v₂² - v₁²). Velocity and therefore volumetric flow Q are proportional to √(ΔP / ρ), requiring square root extraction in the differential pressure flow transmitter.
  - Q: Why is beta ratio β constrained between 0.20 and 0.70 in ISO 5167?
    A: At β < 0.20, the restriction is extremely tight, producing severe permanent pressure loss and pipe wall wear. At β > 0.70, the measured pressure drop ΔP becomes very small and sensitive to upstream velocity profile distortion, increasing metering uncertainty.
- **Curricular Tags**: Orifice Plate, ISO 5167, Beta Ratio, Differential Pressure, Square Root Extraction

---

## Euler-Bernoulli Beam Deflection, Shear & Moment
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/beam-bending
- **Discipline**: Structural Mechanics (civil) | **Level**: Fundamentals | **Badge**: AISC 360 / Eurocode 3
- **Overview**: Solve differential beam equilibrium under combined concentrated point loads and uniformly distributed loads (UDL). Inspect elastic deformed shapes, maximum fiber stresses, and verify AISC L/360 deflection serviceability.
- **Physical Law**: Euler-Bernoulli Beam Theory & Hooke’s Law
- **Governing Formulation**: `EI \frac{d^4 w}{dx^4} = q(x), \quad \sigma_{max} = \frac{M_{max} y}{I}`
- **Equation Description**: Euler-Bernoulli 4th-order beam equation and flexural stress formula.
- **Referenced Standards**: AISC 360-16 / Eurocode 3 (EN 1993-1-1) / ASTM A36 (Structural Steel Design)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: From Euler-Bernoulli beam theory: planar cross sections remain plane and normal to the deformed centroidal axis, yielding strain ε = -y (d²w/dx²). Combining with Hooke’s law σ = E ε and moment equilibrium d²M/dx² = -q(x) gives the 4th-order ODE: EI (d⁴w/dx⁴) = q(x). Integrating with pinned-pinned boundary conditions w(0)=w(L)=0 yields midspan deflection δ_max = (P L³)/(48 E I) + (5 q L⁴)/(384 E I).
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: AISC W250×67 benchmark: Span L = 6.0 m, P = 45 kN at midspan, q = 12 kN/m (E = 200 GPa, I = 84.9×10⁻⁶ m⁴). Theoretical midspan deflection δ_mid = 11.93 mm (point) + 11.93 mm (UDL) = 23.86 mm. AISC L/360 allowable limit = 6000/360 = 16.67 mm.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: AISC 360-16 Table L-1 specifies L/360 for floor beams carrying brittle plaster ceilings and L/240 for general structural roof members. Extreme fiber stress σ = M_max y / I must satisfy LRFD strength φ_b M_n where φ_b = 0.90.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Span Length L` (L): Range [2 to 12 m], Default: 6 m. Clear distance between support boundaries
  - `Concentrated Load P` (P): Range [0 to 150 kN], Default: 45 kN. Point load applied along beam span
  - `Load Position` (a): Range [0.5 to 10 m], Default: 3 m. Distance from left support to concentrated load
  - `Uniform Load q` (q): Range [0 to 35 kN/m], Default: 12 kN/m. Continuous distributed self-weight and live load
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Peak Moment (kN·m), Max Deflection (mm), AISC Limit L/360 (mm), Max Stress (MPa)
- **University Course Mapping**: CE-310: Mechanics of Materials | CE-330: Structural Analysis I
- **Standard Textbook References**: Mechanics of Materials (R.C. Hibbeler, 10th Ed., Ch. 6, 12) | Mechanics of Materials (Gere & Goodno, 9th Ed., Ch. 9-10)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: How do Shear Force Diagrams (SFD) and Bending Moment Diagrams (BMD) relate mathematically?
    A: Transverse shear force V(x) equals the first spatial derivative of the bending moment: V(x) = dM/dx. Locations where the shear force crosses zero (V = 0) correspond precisely to local maximum or minimum bending moments along the beam span.
  - Q: What is the AISC L/360 deflection limit criterion?
    A: AISC 360 specifies serviceability live-load deflection limits (commonly L/360 for plastered floors or L/240 for roof structures) to prevent plaster cracking, sagging ponding, and perceived floor bounce under normal occupancy.
  - Q: What fundamental kinematic assumptions govern Euler-Bernoulli beam theory?
    A: Euler-Bernoulli theory assumes cross-sections normal to the neutral axis remain plane and perpendicular to the deformed centroidal axis, neglecting transverse shear deformation (valid for slender beams with span-to-depth ratio L/d > 10).
- **Curricular Tags**: Beam Deflection, AISC 360, SFD & BMD, Euler-Bernoulli, Bending Stress

## Warren & Pratt Truss Bridge Analysis
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/truss-bridge
- **Discipline**: Bridge & Framed Structures (civil) | **Level**: Intermediate | **Badge**: AASHTO LRFD
- **Overview**: Calculates all internal axial forces (tension vs compression) across a 6-bay steel truss bridge as live vehicular traffic traverses the lower deck chord. Verifies compression members against Euler critical column buckling.
- **Physical Law**: Newton’s Static Equilibrium & Euler Column Buckling
- **Governing Formulation**: `\sum \vec{F}_{node} = 0, \quad P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{(K L)^2}`
- **Equation Description**: Nodal static equilibrium and Euler column buckling threshold.
- **Referenced Standards**: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications / AISC 360-16 / Eurocode 1 (EN 1991-2)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Planar pin-jointed truss equilibrium relies on static determinacy: b + r = 2j. At each node, the vector force balance ∑ F_x = 0 and ∑ F_y = 0 is formulated into a global equilibrium matrix [A] {F} = {P}. For compressive members of length L and radius of gyration r_g, Euler column theory establishes the elastic critical buckling capacity: P_cr = (π² E I) / (K L)², where effective length factor K = 1.0 for pinned chord/web joints.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: AASHTO LRFD benchmark: 6-bay Warren truss (span L = 24 m, height H = 4.5 m) with dead load w_d = 15 kN/joint and truck axle P = 80 kN. Nodal reactions and internal forces achieve perfect static balance (∑ F_y = 0.000 kN). Critical compression member verifies Euler buckling factor.
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: AASHTO LRFD specifies member slenderness limit K L / r ≤ 120 for main compression members and ≤ 140 for secondary bracing. Impact dynamic allowance (IM = 33%) is applied to vehicular axle live loads.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Bridge Span L` (L): Range [12 to 36 m], Default: 24 m. Total span length of the truss bridge structure
  - `Truss Depth H` (H): Range [3 to 8 m], Default: 4.5 m. Vertical distance between top and bottom chords
  - `Moving Truck Load` (P_truck): Range [20 to 200 kN], Default: 80 kN. Wheel load of passing heavy vehicle
  - `Dead Load / Joint` (w_d): Range [5 to 40 kN], Default: 15 kN. Permanent deck self-weight per lower node
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Max Tension (kN), Max Compression (kN), Critical Buckling P_cr (kN), Buckling Margin (dimensionless)
- **University Course Mapping**: CE-200: Statics | CE-340: Structural Steel Design
- **Standard Textbook References**: Vector Mechanics for Engineers: Statics (Beer & Johnston, 12th Ed., Ch. 6) | Structural Analysis (Hibbeler, 10th Ed., Ch. 3)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: How does the Method of Joints resolve member axial forces?
    A: Assuming pin-connected nodes and weightless members loaded only at joints, each node constitutes a concurrent coplanar force system in static equilibrium: ∑ F_x = 0 and ∑ F_y = 0. Solving joint by joint yields internal axial tension and compression values.
  - Q: Why do compression members fail by Euler buckling before material yield?
    A: Slender compressive struts experience geometric lateral instability at the critical Euler load P_cr = π² E I / (K L)². If compressive load exceeds P_cr, the member buckles catastrophically even though stress remains well below the steel yield limit σ_y.
- **Curricular Tags**: Method of Joints, Warren Truss, Pratt Truss, Euler Buckling, AASHTO LRFD

## Seismic Base Isolation & Dynamic Multi-Story Response
- **URL**: https://livesimulators.com/simulator/seismic-base-isolation
- **Discipline**: Earthquake Engineering (civil) | **Level**: Advanced | **Badge**: ASCE 7-22 / Eurocode 8
- **Overview**: Simulates horizontal earthquake ground motion shaking a 4-story building frame. Demonstrates how elastomeric base isolators absorb 80%+ of seismic energy through shear strain, elongating natural periods and mitigating inter-story drift.
- **Physical Law**: Newton’s Second Law & Elastomeric Hysteresis
- **Governing Formulation**: `M \ddot{u} + C \dot{u} + K u = -M \ddot{u}_g(t), \quad T_n = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}`
- **Equation Description**: MDOF dynamic equations of motion and natural vibration period.
- **Referenced Standards**: ASCE 7-22 Chapter 17 / FEMA P-1051 / Eurocode 8 (EN 1998-1)
- **Analytical Proof & Mathematical Derivation**: Base isolation shifts the fundamental structure period T_i = 2π √(W / (k_eff g)) well beyond the high-energy spectrum zone (from 0.4s up to 2.5s+). Lead-rubber hysteresis provides energy dissipation with equivalent damping ratio β_eff = (4 Q (D - D_y)) / (2 π k_eff D²), reducing story drift by over 75%.
- **Benchmark Validation Test**: ASCE 7-22 benchmark: 4-story building subjected to 0.45g PGA. Base shear is reduced from fixed-base 1720 kN to isolated 480 kN (72% reduction), keeping peak interstory drift ratio below 0.015 (ASCE 7-22 Table 12.12-1 limit satisfied).
- **Industrial Practical Insights**: Seismic isolation joints must accommodate total maximum displacement D_TM = S_D1 T_i / (4 π² B_M) plus bidirectional torsion. Flexible utility loops (gas, water, electrical) must be designed to withstand up to 400 mm of lateral ground displacement without rupture.
- **Tunable Parameters**:
  - `Ground Accel (PGA)` (PGA): Range [0.1 to 0.8 g], Default: 0.45 g. Peak Ground Acceleration from seismic event
  - `Earthquake Frequency` (f_eq): Range [0.5 to 4 Hz], Default: 1.8 Hz. Dominant frequency of seismic shear wave excitation
  - `LRB Lead Core Dia` (D_lead): Range [80 to 200 mm], Default: 120 mm. Diameter of central hysteretic lead yielding plug
  - `Bearing Damping` (ζ_iso): Range [10 to 30 %], Default: 18 %. Effective equivalent viscous damping ratio of isolator
- **Solved Real-Time Outputs**: Natural Period Tn (s), Base Shear Vb (kN), Roof Drift Δ (mm), ASCE 2% Check (dimensionless)
- **University Course Mapping**: CE-450: Structural Dynamics | CE-540: Earthquake Engineering
- **Standard Textbook References**: Dynamics of Structures: Theory and Applications to Earthquake Engineering (Chopra, 5th Ed., Ch. 13, 20) | Design of Seismic Isolated Structures (Naeim & Kelly)
- **Frequently Asked Questions & Theoretical Concepts**:
  - Q: How does seismic base isolation decouple a building from ground acceleration?
    A: By inserting low-horizontal-stiffness elastomeric bearings at the foundation level, the natural period of the building is lengthened from the resonance range (0.3 - 0.8 s) out to 2.5 - 3.5 s. The superstructure responds nearly as a rigid body with drastically reduced floor accelerations and interstory drift.
  - Q: What is the role of the central lead core in Lead-Rubber Bearings (LRB)?
    A: The central lead core yields plastically at low shear strain (approximately 10 MPa yield stress). As the bearing undergoes horizontal cyclic shear during an earthquake, plastic deformation of the lead produces broad hysteretic loops that dissipate 15% to 25% equivalent viscous damping.
- **Curricular Tags**: Earthquake Dynamics, Base Isolation, Lead-Rubber Bearings, ASCE 7-22, Story Drift
